summary: Introduces bioctal, an alternative to hexadecimal designed to reduce mental effort when a number must be converted to binary by a person. It argues hexadecimal was chosen for four-bit groups but ignores cognitive factors. It is experimental, and appears to be in a humorous spirit.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9226 is an April 1st joke proposing Bioctal, a replacement alphabet for hexadecimal's second group of eight digits. It says the letters' shapes help a person see the corresponding binary pattern.

questions: how does bioctal differ from hexadecimal
subtitle: An April 1st joke proposing Bioctal as an alternative to hexadecimal.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke argues that hexadecimal's letters make it harder for people to convert digits to binary mentally.
tldr.mechanism: Bioctal keeps the first octave as digits 0 through 7 and replaces the second octave with letters chosen as shape-based mnemonics.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9226 is an Experimental joke document proposing a different way to write hexadecimal values.

today: RFC 9226 is Experimental and dated April 1, 2022. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Case Against Hexadecimal
sections.content: RFC 9226 is an April 1st joke about hexadecimal notation. It argues that hexadecimal was adopted because it groups four binary digits, but that its letters A through F are arbitrary and make mental conversion to binary harder. The RFC proposes Bioctal as an alternative alphabet.
sections.plainLanguage: This April 1st joke says hexadecimal is harder to convert in your head because it uses letters for some digits. It proposes a new set of symbols instead.

sections.title: The Bioctal Alphabet
sections.content: Bioctal keeps the first row of the hexadecimal table as digits 0 through 7. It replaces the second row with the letters c, j, z, w, f, s, b, and v. The RFC says these letters are chosen for visual similarities to the digits above them; a letter indicates that the most significant bit is 1.
sections.plainLanguage: Bioctal keeps digits 0 through 7 and uses letters for the next eight values. The RFC says a letter signals that the highest bit is 1.

sections.title: Objections and the Joke
sections.content: The RFC answers objections about the name Bioctal, the established use of hexadecimal, and the fact that Bioctal values do not sort numerically in ASCII order. It gives deliberately exaggerated responses, including suggesting that technicians who dislike Bioctal be assigned work involving binary numbers. Its conclusion continues the same humorous tone.
sections.plainLanguage: The document answers practical objections with deliberately exaggerated replies. These objections and responses are part of the RFC's joke.
